meta.title: Who really said "You will never find justice in a world where criminals make the rules"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. Bob Marley never said “You will never find justice in a world where criminals make the rules.” It’s an unsourced modern saying — Wikiquote files it as misattributed.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You will never find justice in a world where criminals make the rules'?
meta.ogDescription: Bob Marley never said it. There’s no song, interview, or writing behind the line — Wikiquote lists it as misattributed.

answer.label: Not Bob Marley — an unsourced modern saying
answer.authorDates: Popularized online in the 2010s–2020s · no documented author
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Bob Marley writing or saying this in any song, interview, or documented statement. Wikiquote files it under “Misattributed” ↗, noting it spread on protest signs and social-media posts. The true originator is unknown.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: None — not in any song, interview, or writing

source.excerpt: You will never find justice in a world where criminals make the rules.
trail: The line appears in Wikiquote’s “Misattributed” section for Bob Marley ↗, which notes it was “seen on protest signs and social media posts” with no source in his work.
No verified Marley song lyric or interview contains this sentence; it is absent from the sourced portion of his Wikiquote entry ↗.

The wording is unstable across posts — “find justice” vs “get justice,” “rules” vs “laws” — as seen across social-media reshares ↗, consistent with an anonymous aphorism, not a quotation from a fixed text.
source.excerptNote: Also circulated as “…where criminals make the laws” and “You can never get justice…” — the drifting wording is itself a hallmark of an unsourced internet quote rather than a fixed line from a real work.
source.rightsNote: Because the wording cannot be tied to any identifiable work or author, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. It is treated here as an anonymous modern saying of unknown origin, not a published, datable text.

author.name: Bob Marley
author.heading: The name the quote is pinned on
author.bio: Bob Marley was the Jamaican singer-songwriter who carried reggae — and songs of resistance like Get Up, Stand Up and Redemption Song — to a global audience. His image as a voice against injustice makes him a natural magnet for pointed political one-liners he never actually wrote. This anti-corruption epigram is one of them: it matches his reputation, but not his documented words.

cite.sourceCitation: “You will never find justice in a world where criminals make the rules.” Attributed to Bob Marley without source; listed as misattributed in “Bob Marley,” Wikiquote, accessed 2026. No primary Marley source located.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘You will never find justice in a world where criminals make the rules’?” Last verified 8 Jul 2026.

copyAttribution: Attributed to Bob Marley, but misattributed — no documented source exists in any of his songs, interviews, or writings. Origin unknown.

misattribution.heading: How Bob Marley got the credit
misattribution.intro: Bob Marley is one of the internet’s favourite magnets for punchy political and feel-good lines he never said. This anti-corruption epigram rides his reputation as a voice against oppression, but no primary source connects it to him.

items.why: Wikiquote lists it under “Misattributed” ↗ with no source, noting it appeared on protest signs and social-media posts rather than in any of his songs or interviews.
Versions swap “find” for “get” and “rules” for “laws” across countless reshares ↗ — a telltale sign of an anonymous saying passed hand to hand, not a line quoted from a real work.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentiment is real and widely shared, but the attribution is not: there is no documented Bob Marley source for it, and Wikiquote flags it as misattributed ↗.

context.heading: Why the line sticks to Marley
lead: Marley’s catalogue — Get Up, Stand Up, Redemption Song, Rebel Music — made him shorthand for standing against a corrupt establishment. A sharp epigram about criminals making the rules slots neatly into that image, which is exactly why it attaches to him so easily and travels so far.

The quote gained fresh traction during 2010s–2020s political protests, appearing on placards and in reshares aimed at governments and figures the poster opposed. Its resonance is genuine; its provenance is not.
context.pull: It sounds like something Marley would say — which is precisely why it isn’t safe to assume he did.
